$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2\}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129622 :question/problem "Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{3}y}\,\text{d}A$, where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,1\le y\le 4\}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{3}y}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{1}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{x}^{3}y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{x}^{3}y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{y}[{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3/2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{y}{[\frac{2}{5}{x}^{5/2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{y}(\frac{2}{5}(1)^{5/2}-\frac{2}{5}(0)^{5/2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{2}{5}\sqrt{y}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{2}{5}\sqrt{y}\,\text{d}y & =\frac{2}{5}{\int }_{1}^{4}{y}^{1/2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{[\frac{2{y}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\cdot \frac{2}{3}((4)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{4}{15}(8-1) \\  & =\frac{28}{15}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186127213 :answer-field/correct 17592186127218 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-5a0ea10f-00cc-5f1e-9234-e05424315508" :question/id #uuid "5a0ea10f-00cc-5f1e-9234-e05424315508" :question/math-academy-id "q-73595" :question/problem "Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{2x}{{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}A,$ where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 4,\,1\le y\le 2\}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:      

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2x}{{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{2x}{{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{2x}{{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{2}{{y}^{4}}[{\int }_{2}^{4}x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{2}{{y}^{4}}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{2}^{4}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{2}{{y}^{4}}(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{12}{{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{12}{{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y & ={[-\frac{4}{{y}^{3}}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =-\frac{4}{{2}^{3}}+\frac{4}{{1}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-27b03b87-7f60-5a41-9452-146569702c1e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-27b03b87-7f60-5a41-9452-146569702c1e" :answer-field/id #uuid "27b03b87-7f60-5a41-9452-146569702c1e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1f8087da-0be9-5661-8053-ef364f6d08fe" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b2329388-28ae-5d8d-9a05-1bffa3cfe3a6" "answer-258eca96-5244-5ca3-b0df-8541f47f4e9b" "answer-6d559819-b00a-5b69-960c-d3f8320ab0a2" "answer-1f8087da-0be9-5661-8053-ef364f6d08fe" "answer-87b99526-1110-5b37-a9b1-d2cd1aa88253"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b2329388-28ae-5d8d-9a05-1bffa3cfe3a6" :answer/id #uuid "b2329388-28ae-5d8d-9a05-1bffa3cfe3a6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-258eca96-5244-5ca3-b0df-8541f47f4e9b" :answer/id #uuid "258eca96-5244-5ca3-b0df-8541f47f4e9b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6d559819-b00a-5b69-960c-d3f8320ab0a2" :answer/id #uuid "6d559819-b00a-5b69-960c-d3f8320ab0a2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1f8087da-0be9-5661-8053-ef364f6d08fe" :answer/id #uuid "1f8087da-0be9-5661-8053-ef364f6d08fe" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-87b99526-1110-5b37-a9b1-d2cd1aa88253" :answer/id #uuid "87b99526-1110-5b37-a9b1-d2cd1aa88253" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ec2c5b36-cc64-59b6-941f-e3ef54e2e8b8" :question/id #uuid "ec2c5b36-cc64-59b6-941f-e3ef54e2e8b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-72136" :question/problem "Which of the following equalities are true given that
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,-1\le y\le 1\}.$

I. ${∬}_{D}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$

II. ${∬}_{D}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$

III. ${∬}_{D}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y$" :question/worked-solution "We notice that:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the region of integration is rectangular, we can simply swap the order of integration. This gives

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x.

The **double integral** of $f(x,y)$ over $R,$ denoted

$$
\iint\limits_{R}{ f(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}A},
$$

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} {{(3-x^2-y^2) \, \mathrm{d}A}},

$$

$$

17592186130374 :tutorial/content "Let's once again consider the integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D}{ { (x^2+y^2) \, \mathrm{d}A}}
$$

over the rectangular domain 

$$
D=[0,1] \times [0,1] = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

Similar to definite integrals of single-variable functions, this double integral can be defined as the limit of a Riemann sum, as follows:

$$
\iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}} = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{n,\,\,m \to \infty } \sum\limits_{j = 1}^n {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^m {f\big( {x_i^*,y_j^*} \big)\,\Delta x_i \Delta y_j} }
$$

Notice that in the above summation, we could have instead summed over the $j$'s first and then the $i$'s, giving

$$
\iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}} = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{m,\,\,n \to \infty } \sum\limits_{i = 1}^m {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^n {f\big( {x_i^*,y_j^*} \big)\,\Delta y_j \Delta x_i} },
$$

and this would result in an iterated integral in the reverse order: 

$$
\iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}}  
= \int_0^1\int_0^1 f(x,y)\ \mathrm{d}  y\,  \mathrm{d}  x.
$$

 

Regardless of the order in which we carry out the integration, the answer will always be the same!

Moreover, *provided that the region $D$ is rectangular*, we can swap the order of integration. This means that if 

$$
D=[a,b] \times [c,d] = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: a \leq x \leq b, \: c \leq y \leq d \big\},
$$

then

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{c}^{d}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,y)\text{ }dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{c}^{d}f(x,y)\text{ }dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "21451089-e080-55c2-acf5-60d200c5ee21" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3859 :tutorial/title "The Order of Integration for Double Integrals on a Rectangular Domain"} :step/id #uuid "e9f89a44-c08e-51d9-95f7-d73be3535606" :step/math-academy-id 22621 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130022}} {:db/id 17592186130043 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130381 :tutorial/content "A **repeated integral**, also known as an **iterated integral,** is an integral in which we carry out repeated integration with respect to different variables. An example of a repeated integral is as follows:

$$
\int_0^1\int_0^1 ye^{xy}\,\textrm d x\,\textrm d y
$$

To evaluate this integral, we first integrate with respect to the inner variable $x,$ and then with respect to the outer variable $y$. We can write this more explicitly as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We now carry out the integration. First, we integrate with respect to $x,$ *treating $y$ as a constant*. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{y{e}^{xy}}{y}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{e}^{xy}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y}-{e}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y}-1\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y}-1\,\text{d}y & ={[{e}^{y}-y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[e-1]-[1-0] \\  & =e-2.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that

$$
\int_0^1\int_0^1 ye^{xy}\,\textrm d x\,\textrm d y = e-2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ab6d3983-ce7d-5e80-9dfc-ae0644ac5030" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3904 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b2b10cfb-2130-565a-9f4e-f0f29bef13a2" :step/math-academy-id 23088 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130020}} {:db/id 17592186130110 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130412 :tutorial/content "Consider the surface $z= f(x,y) = 3-x^2-y^2,$ defined over the following rectangle:

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "21451089-e080-55c2-acf5-60d200c5ee21" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3859 :tutorial/title "The Order of Integration for Double Integrals on a Rectangular Domain"} :step/id #uuid "e9f89a44-c08e-51d9-95f7-d73be3535606" :step/math-academy-id 22621 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130022}} {:db/id 17592186130022 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129166 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128985 :question/id #uuid "e51c2aa9-027b-5b23-bcaf-805804a8de9c" :question/math-academy-id "e-6099"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d8f012d0-444a-5035-8a72-a053de312d63" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129843} {:db/id 17592186129844} {:db/id 17592186265759} {:db/id 17592186265760} {:db/id 17592186339061} {:db/id 17592186339067} {:db/id 17592186342027} {:db/id 17592186382235} {:db/id 17592186382277}] :knowledge-point/title "Changing the Order of Integration"} :step/id #uuid "def04952-960b-574f-ad97-fdf9decfb2de" :step/math-academy-id 22584} {:db/id 17592186130374 :tutorial/content "Let's once again consider the integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D}{ { (x^2+y^2) \, \mathrm{d}A}}
$$

over the rectangular domain 

$$
D=[0,1] \times [0,1] = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

Similar to definite integrals of single-variable functions, this double integral can be defined as the limit of a Riemann sum, as follows:

$$
\iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}} = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{n,\,\,m \to \infty } \sum\limits_{j = 1}^n {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^m {f\big( {x_i^*,y_j^*} \big)\,\Delta x_i \Delta y_j} }
$$

Notice that in the above summation, we could have instead summed over the $j$'s first and then the $i$'s, giving

$$
\iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}} = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{m,\,\,n \to \infty } \sum\limits_{i = 1}^m {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^n {f\big( {x_i^*,y_j^*} \big)\,\Delta y_j \Delta x_i} },
$$

and this would result in an iterated integral in the reverse order: 

$$
\iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}}  
= \int_0^1\int_0^1 f(x,y)\ \mathrm{d}  y\,  \mathrm{d}  x.
$$

 

Regardless of the order in which we carry out the integration, the answer will always be the same!

Moreover, *provided that the region $D$ is rectangular*, we can swap the order of integration. This means that if 

$$
D=[a,b] \times [c,d] = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: a \leq x \leq b, \: c \leq y \leq d \big\},
$$

then

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{c}^{d}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,y)\text{ }dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{c}^{d}f(x,y)\text{ }dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "21451089-e080-55c2-acf5-60d200c5ee21" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3859 :tutorial/title "The Order of Integration for Double Integrals on a Rectangular Domain"} {:db/id 17592186130381 :tutorial/content "A **repeated integral**, also known as an **iterated integral,** is an integral in which we carry out repeated integration with respect to different variables. An example of a repeated integral is as follows:

$$
\int_0^1\int_0^1 ye^{xy}\,\textrm d x\,\textrm d y
$$

To evaluate this integral, we first integrate with respect to the inner variable $x,$ and then with respect to the outer variable $y$. We can write this more explicitly as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We now carry out the integration. First, we integrate with respect to $x,$ *treating $y$ as a constant*. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{y{e}^{xy}}{y}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{e}^{xy}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y}-{e}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y}-1\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y}-1\,\text{d}y & ={[{e}^{y}-y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[e-1]-[1-0] \\  & =e-2.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that

$$
\int_0^1\int_0^1 ye^{xy}\,\textrm d x\,\textrm d y = e-2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ab6d3983-ce7d-5e80-9dfc-ae0644ac5030" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3904 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186130412 :tutorial/content "Consider the surface $z= f(x,y) = 3-x^2-y^2,$ defined over the following rectangle:

$$
R=[0,1] \times [0,1] = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

A sketch of our surface and its domain is shown below.

![](images/1f/1fdf4668c7e89a9a32ee8e655fe5c80c899a04d25a0f342365560f4d9abdd8fd.png)

The **double integral** of $f(x,y)$ over $R,$ denoted

$$
\iint\limits_{R}{ f(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}A},
$$

represents the total *signed* volume bounded between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the planes $x=0, x=1, y=0, y=1.$

It can be shown that the double integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} {{(3-x^2-y^2) \, \mathrm{d}A}},
$$

can be evaluated using the repeated integral 

$$
\displaystyle \int_0^1\int_0^1 (3-x^2-y^2) \, \mathrm{d}  x\,  \mathrm{d}  y.
$$

Notice that we replace $\textrm d A$ with $\textrm d x\,\textrm d y$ when writing our double integral as a repeated integral." :tutorial/id #uuid "b04cc8c6-0b4d-5f4e-9027-892d33558737"
